note: France is the hard case and the interesting one. The découpe follows seams, so several morceaux really are single muscles and can be named exactly — paleron, macreuse à bifteck, rond de gîte, tende de tranche, gîte à la noix, rumsteck, filet, onglet, hampe, joue, aiguillette baronne. But French butchery names pieces, not muscles, and the trade's own cut↔muscle table is the Quizlet BP Boucher deck, which serves a CAPTCHA. So the shoulder's five pieces resolve to two, the neck resolves to none, and the honest answer for the rest is `inferred` with the position quote that was actually published. Two levers did most of the work here beyond what FINDINGS.md already had: VPC article 323's Table 5 footnotes, which pair MQ4 codes with Latin muscles and French cut names, and the UNECE bovine standard reached through mymemory.translated.net's FR/EN parallel segments, which turned out to name muscles for the basses côtes (via `noix de bassecôte`) and to settle the aiguillette baronne = tensor fasciae latae question that FINDINGS.md had recorded as unresolved in both directions.

Canadian nomenclature must not be transferred onto the French macreuse. The atlas models the triceps as one body, so `caput longum` can only be expressed as a portion with a note; the seam between the heads is real but the model cannot hold it.

cuts.dispute: No source consulted names a muscle for the jumeau à bifteck; it is one of the blurb-only shoulder pieces FINDINGS.md flagged, and the French trade's own cut↔muscle table — the Quizlet BP Boucher deck — serves a CAPTCHA. Two positional facts are quotable: gastronomiac puts it `sur le scapulum (palette)` and puts the macreuse `du côté opposé aux jumeaux`, i.e. the two jumeaux are on the scapula side and the macreuse on the humerus side. The muscles are then taken from CFIA's description of the medial-scapula piece (`bas de palette`), which contains teres major, subscapularis and serratus ventralis. That is a bridge across nomenclatures and the assignment should be read as a hypothesis, not a fact. The competing hypothesis, which nothing here settles: this atlas's own description of the cut calls it a long muscle with short fibres lying under the blade, wording that would fit the deltoideus or a triceps head just as well. That description is not a source either.

cuts.dispute: Blurb-only, exactly as FINDINGS.md predicted. The one hard fact any source gives is the bone it lies along: gastronomiac says `situé le long de l'humérus` and glosses the humerus as the bone from shoulder to elbow. Everything along that bone that is not already claimed by the macreuse à bifteck (triceps long head) is what is listed here — the other two triceps heads, the biceps brachii, and the brachialis and anconeus as unmodelled. That is an assignment from position, not from a source, and it overlaps the macreuse à pot-au-feu for the same reason: the French shoulder is carved into five named pieces and only two of them (paleron, macreuse à bifteck) are named to a muscle by anybody.

cuts.dispute: No source names a muscle for the gelatinous macreuse specifically. gastronomiac treats `macreuse à bifteck` and `macreuse gélatineuse` as two grades of one shoulder piece, distinguished by cooking method rather than by anatomy, and UNECE's French segments give only `macreuse` = `shoulder (cushion)` and `macreuse à bifteck` = `shoulder clod`. Since VPC 323 has already claimed the triceps long head for the macreuse à bifteck, what is left of the Calkins `clod heart` mass — the lateral head over the humerus — plus the deltoideus and the shoulder end of the brachiocephalicus is what is assigned here. Position-derived, and it deliberately overlaps the jumeau à pot-au-feu, because no source draws the seam between them.

cuts.dispute: No source names a muscle for the fore shank, and unlike the hind shank there is no Calkins row to lean on — the Calkins table covers 32 muscles ranked for tenderness and contains nothing below the elbow at the front. The whole muscle list is therefore bovine forelimb anatomy: the carpal and digital flexors and extensors wrapped round the radius-ulna, of which the atlas models only the extensor carpi radialis. Bounds, by contrast, are standard: CFIA's French definition of the jarret avant cuts just dorsal to the elbow at the distal end of the humerus and follows the olecranon, and UNECE gives `jarret avant 5030` = `foreshank 5030`.

cuts.dispute: The collier is the clearest case in the French table of a cut whose documented contents are **butcher's pieces, not muscles**: gastronomiac lists `la veine maigre, de la veine grasse et d'une partie de la griffe`, FINDINGS.md records `la salière, la veine grasse et la veine maigre` from another source, and UNECE's French segments have no entry for `collier` at all — mymemory returns `necklace` and `clamp`. Two pieces of real evidence sit either side of it and neither is a definition. UNECE names m. serratus ventralis, m. rhomboideus and m. splenius for the square-cut chuck once the basses côtes are removed, which is the primal immediately behind the collier, and VPC 323 gives `demi-épineux` as the French butchery name for M. semispinalis capitis — the modelled `complexus` — without saying which cut that piece is sold in. The list here is therefore the cervical musculature from bovine anatomy, weighted by those two hints. Bounds are the seven cervical vertebrae, per gastronomiac.

cuts.dispute: The source is explicit that the cut is the masseter and **only** the masseter (`composée uniquement de la masse musculaire des masséters`), which is why the temporalis and the pterygoids are not listed even though they are chewing muscles on the same skull — they are not in this piece. Sold in France as an abat rather than as a carcass cut, which is why no meat-cut specification defines it and the grade is trade rather than standard.
